Photograph: Barry Iverson/Alamy Oil Oil prices plunge and Europe’s stock markets rally after Trump calls off Iran strikes Brent crude drops by 5% after US president said talks on Middle East peace deal would resume Business live – latest updates Julia Kollewe Mon 3 Aug 2026 04.44 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 05.16 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Crude oil prices fell sharply and European stock markets rallied on Monday after Donald Trump cancelled planned strikes on Iran to focus on negotiations for a peace deal. Brent crude was trading 5% lower at $83.50 a barrel by mid-morning, after falling as low as $81.55 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate dropped more than $5 to $79.47 a barrel. Both global oil benchmarks jumped more than 20% in July after fighting between the US and Iran resumed, and as attacks on several tankers in the strait of Hormuz revived fears for the safety of vessels transiting the important shipping passage. UK economy faces recession if strait of Hormuz remains closed, EY warns - business live Read more Trump said late on Saturday on his Truth Social platform that Iran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked for time to complete a deal that would lead to “the Immediate, Complete and Total” reopening of the strait and “an end to Iran’s nuclear threat”. On Sunday, he said talks with Tehran would start on Monday . Kathleen Brooks, the research director of the broker XTB, said the drop in oil prices should help support markets. “This will ease inflation fears and could also act as a dampener on bond yields, which rose sharply last week, especially at the long end, where 30-year US Treasury yields jumped to their highest level for 19 years ,” she added. In a positive start to August, European shares edged higher. The pan-European Stoxx 600 index rose 0.4%. Energy stocks declined 2%, while travel and leisure shares gained 2.1%. Tony Sycamore, a market analyst at the investment platform IG, said: “The bigger focus is whether this week turns into a rinse and repeat of last week – with hopes of a deal collapsing as Iran digs in its heels and continues to leverage its control over the strait, potentially through an attack on a US base or a tanker transiting the waterway.” Two tankers laden with Saudi oil crossed the Bab el-Mandeb strait out of the Red Sea over the weekend, while traffic in the strait of Hormuz slowed after reports of vessel attacks, according to shipping data. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre has reported three more tanker attacks since Saturday. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Preview latest after newsletter promotion On Sunday, the oil cartel Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies, known as Opec+, agreed to increase oil production by about 188,000 barrels a day from September, unwinding output cuts. However, because of the export disruptions from the Gulf, Russia and Kazakhstancaused by the Iran and Ukraine wars, production increases by Opec+ have had little impact on prices. Elsewhere in the markets, the Japanese yen hit a three-month high after Tokyo and Washington launched a joint operation to support the currency. https://voiceofvienna.org/austria-sees-m.text: Austria has recorded more deportations than new asylum applications for the first time in over 20 years, marking a significant shift in the country’s migration landscape. The latest figures from the Interior Ministry show a sharp decline in asylum requests, reflecting a trend that officials say has been developing since 2023. Between January and June, 4,903 people applied for asylum in Austria, down 44 percent from around 8,800 applications during the same period last year. According to the ministry, the number is the lowest recorded in nearly 23 years. Family reunification also remained limited, with only 48 people entering the country through the program by the end of June. Interior Minister Gerhard Karner said the figures point to what he described as a “turning point” in Austria’s migration policy. More than 7,000 people either left the country through deportation or other forms of removal during the first half of the year. Among them were 2,200 people with asylum-related status, exceeding the roughly 2,000 first-time asylum applications submitted by newly arrived migrants. Karner called the development “negative migration,” arguing that the trend should be preserved through continued border controls and immigration measures. Of the total asylum applications, only 2,016 came from people newly arriving in Austria. The remainder included applications from children born in the country, family reunification cases, and repeat applicants. Nearly half of all applicants were minors. Syria and Afghanistan remained the largest countries of origin, each accounting for about one-quarter of all applications. However, among newly arrived asylum seekers, Afghans formed the largest group, followed by Syrians and Iranians. Austria currently has 15,278 asylum cases awaiting decisions, with nearly half involving Syrian nationals. While applicants from Iran had the highest approval rate at 76 percent, the recognition rate for Syrians fell sharply to 32 percent, compared with 67 percent last year. Officials also noted that Austria, alongside Poland, has recorded the steepest decline in asylum applications across the European Union. Meanwhile, more than 45,000 people remain in Austria’s basic support system, the majority of them Ukrainians displaced by war. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images View image in fullscreen MI6’s headquarters seen from across the Thames in London. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images Espionage The Bond effect? How MI6 fascinates spy watchers around the world Britain’s spooks take quiet satisfaction from survey ranking Secret Intelligence Service Europe’s top espionage agency Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor Sat 8 Aug 2026 07.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google M I6 has the swagger of James Bond; its French equivalent, DGSE, the complexities of the television drama Le Bureau. The film and TV shows may be fictional, but a survey run by a French magazine that placed the British spy agency above the French as No 1 across all of Europe this week is not. L’Express , a news weekly, conducted a Eurovision-style poll of 60 current and former spies from across the continent, plus the CIA and Israel’s Mossad. Each was asked to rank their top five foreign intelligence agencies, in secret, naturally enough. MI6 was first with 251 points ahead of DGSE on 169, with other agencies trailing behind. The result did not surprise Alexandra Saviana, a deputy editor at the publication, specialising in defence and intelligence, but the margin of victory did. “It is a huge point gap,” she said, reflecting the opinions of insiders and allies, 17 of whom are or were agency chiefs in a interconnected, covert ecosystem. View image in fullscreen Desmond Llewelyn as Q and Roger Moore as James Bond in The Spy Who Loved Me (1977). Photograph: Sportsphoto/Allstar At MI6’s headquarters in Vauxhall, London, there has been no sign of a public reaction from its chief, Blaise Metreweli . But there is a quiet satisfaction at the unexpected verdict, not least because the agency values how it is perceived by both allies and adversaries. “Reputation matters a lot in the espionage game,” said a former Whitehall insider. “British spies fascinate Europe , and beyond,” L’Express explained in its cover story. Saviana added that MI6’s success in the poll was principally down to its record in recruiting and running high-level human sources over generations: a focus on human intelligence in an era dominated by technology, intercepts and satellite monitoring. “The British have the ability to play the long game, to bet on sources over 10 years, a bit like the Russians,” a former French DGSE spy told the magazine, adding “and they have a penchant for underhand tactics” without revealing what they meant. One ex-spy voiced scepticism about the survey and added that a human intelligence service such as MI6 was only as good as the high-value agents on its books. Under Richard Moore , MI6’s previous chief, there were worries that it no longer had enough. Others, including Saviana, accept that greater credit might have been given to MI6’s sister agency, the signals intelligence experts at GCHQ, but it was not in the poll. MI6’s reputation among its peers, the French publication said, was built on “long standing tradition”, including recruiting cold war assets, most notably the KGB’s Oleg Gordievsky , a double agent through late 1970s and early 80s, who helped convince Margaret Thatcher to take Mikhail Gorbachev seriously before he had to be dramatically smuggled into Finland in 1985, his cover finally blown. View image in fullscreen Ronald Reagan meeting Oleg Gordievsky, an MI6 cold war asset, in the White House, 1987. Photograph: Eraza Collection/Alamy Not every mole evaded capture. Alireza Akbari, a former Iranian deputy defence minister who had become a British citizen, was arrested on a return to Iran in 2019 and executed in 2023. Prior to his death, he confessed to being an MI6 agent. Though the confessions appeared coerced, spies from a number of countries indicated he was the person who had passed on the existence of the Fordow nuclear enrichment site in 2008. In the run-up to the 2003 Iraq war, MI6 was accused of simplistically supporting the case for war, promoting what turned out to be false sources, claiming that Iraq’s leader, Saddam Hussein, could attack UK targets within “45 minutes”, and relied on one source who described supposed chemical weapons devices that were remarkably similar to one in the Hollywood movie The Rock . It was a low point. L’Express argued that MI6 had rehabilitated itself in the run-up to the Ukraine war in February 2022, correctly warning in conjunction with the CIA that Russia was about to invade, while French and German counterparts were sceptical up until the last minute, having misjudged the situation. The chief of the German BND agency even flew into Kyiv the day before the invasion, seemingly unprepared. It reflects MI6’s close and longstanding relationship with the CIA, part of the wider Five Eyes arrangements for intelligence sharing, between the US, UK, Australia, Canada and New Zealand, that are the envy of continental Europe, even allowing for the complexities posed by Donald Trump’s chaotic presidency. “Every other country wants to say they are the sixth eye,” Saviana said. Fiction also has its advantages. Gordon Corera, a co-presenter of The Rest is Classified podcast, recalled that a former MI6 chief once told him a story of a young officer going somewhere far flung, not knowing whether the person he was trying to cultivate spoke English. “As he walked into the room the contact extended his hand and said: ‘Hello, Mr Bond.’ The former chief remarked: ‘I doubt if he would have received such a warm welcome if he’d been from the Belgian secret service.’” Explore more on these topics Espionage MI6 Europe UK security and counter-terrorism James Bond news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: ‘The intimidation seen in England and the AfD’s extremism are two sides of the same coin’: an anti-migrant protest in Dover, 5 September 2026. Photograph: Ay_audits/Youtube View image in fullscreen ‘The intimidation seen in England and the AfD’s extremism are two sides of the same coin’: an anti-migrant protest in Dover, 5 September 2026. Photograph: Ay_audits/Youtube Opinion The far right The Guardian view on the far right’s real weapon: it is the politics of powerlessness Editorial From Dover to Saxony-Anhalt, extremists thrive when voters believe established parties can no longer deliver security, prosperity or meaningful change Mon 7 Sep 2026 13.48 EDT Last modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 14.44 EDT Share W hat links the thuggish masked agitation in southern England this weekend and the far-right Alternative für Deutschland’s (AfD) best-ever result in a German state – where it more than doubled the 21% vote it received five years ago? Several hundred men in balaclavas blocking an A road are not the same as a party winning a landslide election. But both events draw on the idea that the political system has lost control. The extremists in Dover and Portsmouth dramatise this claim; the electoral result in Germany threatens to institutionalise it. The prospect of Germany’s first far-right-led state government since the second world war carries real consequences. In Saxony-Anhalt it could see power handed to a party hostile to migrants, Islam, LGBTQ+ rights and climate policy. Alarmingly, it has senior figures linked to former neo-Nazi groups. About 170,000 foreign nationals live among 2 million people in Saxony-Anhalt – and roughly a fifth of the state’s doctors were born abroad. The grim paradox is that an AfD government could oversee the very state intelligence service that has classified the party as “ rightwing extremist ”. In England, the “ Patriot Platform ” agitation is far-right vigilantism that claims it will “stop the boats” if the authorities won’t. The AfD is a political party which presents its success as a repudiation of established parties that, it claims, have failed – most notably on immigration. The intimidation seen in England and the AfD’s extremism are, however, two sides of the same coin: a broader politics in which migration is felt to embody a sense of powerlessness – not just over borders but over state institutions, economic change and national identity. View image in fullscreen Ulrich Siegmund of the AfD. Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPA The AfD polls highest in Germany’s eastern states . These have a post-reunification history of population loss and high unemployment . Britain has its own political geography and history. The small boats are a live political issue. More than 33,000 people arrived by that route in the year to June 2026. Nearly all will claim asylum. But arrivals were 23% lower than the previous year. The street escalation is occurring as numbers are falling. Across Europe, the far right keeps rising because immigration has become a test of whether states can still govern effectively. Cutting migrant numbers or asylum claims does not lessen the issue’s potency. Studies suggest that, in Germany, political alienation is more important to AfD support than deprivation. That is also why, in Britain, using facts alone – that crossings are falling, or that migrants aren’t responsible for NHS waiting lists or stagnant wages – may have little electoral effect. The reality answers the far right’s argument, but doesn’t dispel the deeper belief that the country is becoming ungovernable . Borders, in that sense, are a symptom of a bigger problem: voters increasingly distrust democracy to make things happen for them. In Germany, politicians can point to the constitutional settlement and coalition arithmetic and say that their hands are tied. In Britain, they defer to the bond markets and the Bank of England. The language is different, but the message can sound the same: you can vote for change, but the government is limited in what it can achieve. The answer is not to pretend that inflation or legal constraints are irrelevant. It is to show that they do not amount to a permanent veto on democratic choice. Tom Chambers for Netroots Radio Tom Chambers for Netroots Radio The West Coast Cookbook & Speakeasy Podcast Archive Your intrepid chef/ownerNeeta Lind Neeta Lind “A little bit of jambalaya, a little bit of spice in your life.” – Chef Justice Putnam Fire Pit Soir, Forest Grove, CalifJustice Putnam Justice Putnam Metro Shrimp & Grits 3 cups water 2 teaspoons salt 1 cup coarsely ground grits 2 cups whole milk 2 pounds uncooked 22 to 26 count shrimp, peeled and deveined salt to taste 1 pinch hot smoked Hungarian paprika, or to taste 1 lemon, zest and juiced 2 tablespoons lemon thyme 1 pound andouille sausage, cut into 1/4-inch slices 5 slices hickory smoked bacon 1 medium green bell pepper, chopped 1 medium red bell pepper, chopped 1 medium yellow bell pepper, chopped 1 cup chopped onion 1 teaspoon minced garlic ¼ cup butter ¼ cup all-purpose flour 1 cup chicken broth 1 tablespoon Worcestershire sauce 1 cup shredded sharp Tillamook Cheddar cheese Bring water and 2 teaspoons salt to a boil in a heavy saucepan over medium-high heat. Whisk grits into the boiling water, and then whisk in whole milk. Reduce heat to medium-low and simmer, stirring occasionally, until grits are thickened and tender, 15 to 20 minutes. Set aside and keep warm. Sprinkle shrimp with salt and hot smoked paprika to taste. Add lemon juice, toss to combine, and set aside to marinate. Place sausage slices in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Cook, stirring occasionally, until browned, 5 to 8 minutes. Remove sausage from the skillet. Add bacon to the same skillet and increase heat to medium-high. Cook until evenly browned, about 5 minutes per side. Transfer bacon to paper towels to drain, then chop or crumble when cool enough to handle. Leave bacon drippings in the skillet. Add bell peppers, onion, and garlic to the bacon drippings; cook and stir until onion is translucent, about 8 minutes. Stir cooked sausage and marinated shrimp into the skillet with the cooked vegetables. Turn off the heat and set aside. Melt butter in a small saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in flour, stirring to create a smooth roux. Turn heat to low and cook, stirring constantly, until mixture is golden brown in color, 8 to 10 minutes. Pour the roux over the sausage, shrimp, and vegetables. Place the skillet over medium heat, add chicken broth, bacon, and Worcestershire sauce, and stir to combine. Cook until sauce thickens up and shrimp turn opaque and bright pink, about 8 minutes. Just before serving, mix sharp Cheddar cheese into grits until melted and grits are creamy and light yellow. Serve shrimp mixture over cheese grits. Sprinkle lemon zest and lemon thyme over shrimp and grits. Bon Appétit! (Lockheed Martin graphic) During floods in September 2024, Polish Black Hawk® helicopters flew equipment and personnel into the affected region and evacuated over 100 people. In July, production began in Mielec on Europe’s first S-70 Firehawk helicopters that will go to the Czech Republic. Twelve European countries now operate some version of the Black Hawk for mission sets as diverse as the nations who fly them. In a time of geopolitical tension along NATO’s eastern flank, an armed kit can now turn trusty Black Hawk helicopters into attack Hawks – in a matter of hours and at a fraction of the cost of a dedicated attack helicopter. Sikorsky, a Lockheed Martin company, is offering modular kits with both close support and precision strike configurations that convert a UH-60M or S-70i Black Hawk helicopter from a utility aircraft into an armed one, then back again when the mission changes. The kits support two to six weapons stations and do not reduce the aircraft’s passenger or cargo capacity. The Armed Black Hawk delivers the full medium-category mission set in a single, combat-proven airframe – airmobile assault, close support, medical evacuation, ISR, and tactical lift – maximizing operational flexibility while eliminating the need for separate fleet types and taking advantage of a worldwide sustainment network “Having a single aircraft that can seamlessly transition from high-intensity strike to humanitarian rescue gives any nation a decisive operational edge while dramatically cutting lifecycle costs,” said Ken Demaree, Sikorsky’s Army and Air Force Systems vice president. “The Black Hawk helicopter proves yet again that it is the world’s most versatile helicopter.” The armed Black Hawk kits are designed to interface with a broader set of Black Hawk helicopter upgrades already underway with the U.S. Army, including an improved turbine engine, larger fuel tanks, autonomy options and expanded payload capability. The goal, Demaree said, is a platform that can absorb next-generation sensors, weapons and autonomous flight control packages without major structural changes. “The Black Hawk helicopter will fill mission gaps for the next half century, no matter the theater of operations,” Demaree said. “As we modernize the airframe, we are future-proofing a platform that can adapt to emerging threats and requirements.” Armed Black Hawk equipped with one of several available weapons configurations, demonstrating how a single airframe can deliver strike, casualty evacuation, ISR and utility capabilities. (Lockheed Martin graphic) The economics of a shared fleet A dedicated attack helicopter fleet requires specially trained pilots and mechanics, on top of a separate supply chain, layered onto a service that may already be stretched thin. Sikorsky’s answer is a cost-effective kit that arms the helicopter operators already fly. The kits are available as an option on new aircraft and as a retrofit to UH-60 and S-70 fleets already in service. Because the armed and unarmed configurations share 95 percent of common parts, crews train on one cockpit layout and maintainers service one fleet instead of two. For a budget-conscious air arm, that adds up to fewer training pipelines and spare-parts inventories, and a lower total-ownership cost spread across a single aircraft doing both utility and attack work. Armed Black Hawk at a glance: Close Support Mission Kit: Post penetration fire support against light armor and dismounted troops – perfect for rapid reaction assault and close support. Precision Strike Mission Kit: Penetration attacks on hardened targets, air defense suppression, and precision strike for high-value objectives Reconfiguration time: Fewer than three hours to convert to attack configuration; minutes to remove, using tool-free latching hardware Even with the wing installed and a weapons load aboard, the aircraft still carries 11 fully equipped troops or 3,000 pounds of internal cargo. Mount points: Two to six available configurations Compatible weapons: 7.62mm machine guns, .50-cal GP 19 guns, M261 rocket pods, HELLFIRE II, JAGM, APKWS and Spike NLOS missiles, plus a Modular Effects Launcher for other air-launched effects All of which can be added to the workhorse helicopter the world trusts, with a proven service record of 15 million flight hours, crash-worthy airframe and redundant systems. “The Armed Black Hawk transforms the Black Hawk from a pure utility platform into a multi-role strike asset,” Demaree said. Built in Poland, flown across the continent NATO members agreed at The Hague in June 2025 to reach 5 percent of gross domestic product on defense and security spending by 2035, signaling a mandate to prioritize their security as Ukraine defends itself against Russia. Much of that commitment covers sustaining and modernizing equipment already in service. A share of that equipment is already European built. PZL Mielec, a Lockheed Martin company and one of Poland’s largest aircraft manufacturers, has produced Black Hawk helicopters since 2010 for 18 customers in 11 countries. Sikorsky named Czech firm Česká letecká servisní a certified European Union distribution center for Black Hawk parts, and the Czech Firehawk aircraft now in production are being built in partnership with that company. Romania acquired its S-70 fleet through an EU-funded program and received an additional aircraft in December 2025 under rescEU, the bloc’s shared emergency reserve, which can be dispatched to other member states at the European Union’s request. The result is that an armed Black Hawk arrives into infrastructure that already exists, with an airframe built in Poland, sustained through distributors in Poland and the Czech Republic, and already flown by European nations. “Every helicopter that leaves Mielec goes to work: floods, fires, medical transport, border patrol. Our operators know this aircraft because they have flown it in the worst conditions their countries have faced. The armed configuration is the same helicopter, made in Europe, with one more mission added to its arsenal.” -Janusz Zakrecki, PZL Mielec president and general director. https://www.theguardian.com/news/audio/2.text: 00:00:00 00:00:00 Today in Focus Sally Rooney Why terrorism laws stopped Sally Rooney selling books in the UK – podcast The bestselling author says her books will no longer be supplied to UK bookshops over fears of prosecution. Zoe Williams and Haroon Siddique report More ways to listen Apple podcasts Spotify RSS Feed Download Presented by Nosheen Iqbal with Zoe Williams and Haroon Siddique ; produced by Ruth Abrahams , Eleanor Biggs and Rudi Zygadlo Mon 19 Oct 2026 22.00 EDT Share For now there might be a copy or two of Intermezzo left kicking around in your local bookshop – snap it up if you haven’t already, because soon that will be it. Last year, Sally Rooney said she would be using her royalties to support Palestine Action , a group that is proscribed as a terrorist organisation under UK law. Since then, thousands of people have been arrested for supporting the group. Now, faced with the risk of prosecution under terrorism legislation, Rooney and her publishers have decided to stop supplying her books to retailers in the UK. Over the weekend, hundreds of authors signed an open letter supporting her. The rightwing press, meanwhile, have called Rooney a “tedious and malicious” “posturing ingrate”. Zoe Williams explains the furore surrounding one of the most successful novelists of her generation, while Haroon Siddique tells Nosheen Iqbal how Rooney’s stance could affect the supreme court’s ruling on Palestine Action.
